newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe's doctors strike paralyses hospitals.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe's doctors strike paralyses hospitals.

text.p: Zimbabwe's two major government hospitals stayed paralysed on Thursday, the third day of a strike by junior doctors and other medical staff over the arrest of two colleagues and the firing of thousands of nurses.
Harare Hospital, the southern African country's largest, was hardly functional, with exhausted consultants saying they were unable to continue work without assistance.
"Harare (hospital) is almost at a standstill. The consultants are thinking of walking out," said one senior doctor who refused to be named.
Parirenyatwa Hospital, also in the capital Harare, was virtually deserted, with senior administration staff locked up in meetings with government officials over the strike.
"The situation is bad, not bright at all," one of the officials said.

At Chitungwiza hospital, 40 km (25 miles) south of Harare, superintendent Dick Chifamba said the hospital was also no longer admitting new patients as it was battling to cope and had closed most wards.
The junior doctors, physiotherapists and operating theatre staff went on strike on Tuesday to protest against the arrest of two of their colleagues for inciting a two-week nurses' strike.
Doctors Farai Jiah and Austin Bene -- both leaders of the state Hospitals Doctors Association who were arrested early this week on charges of inciting the strike -- were freed on Wednesday.
Harare magistrate Lazaraus Murendo said he needed time to decide whether to refer their case to the Supreme Court as their lawyer had raised constitutional issues during an initial remand hearing.

One of the strikers said the work stoppage would continue until the government of President Robert Mugabe unconditionally reinstates about 10,000 nurses it fired last week after they defied an order to return to work addresses their demands for higher pay and negotiates their working conditions.
Mugabe declined to talk to reporters on Wednesday after opening a Z$23 million ($2 million) private clinic in Harare built by a consortium of black doctors.
Health and Child Welfare Minister Timothy Stamps also declined to discuss the issue, referring all questions to the labour ministry where officials were locked in meetings with union representatives.
Opposition parties and local human rights groups slammed Mugabe's government for mishandling the crisis, saying its high-handedness had worsened the situation, costing patients' lives.
"The government must resolve this situation urgently because people are dying," Zimrights, the country's main human rights watchdog, said in a statement.
